editions.title: Huang returns to Nvidia as AI rout hits Asia and Nato meets over Poland
editions.notification: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia and its shares jumped 30%. Asian markets are rebounding from the AI rout. Here's what changed.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned, and the shares jumped about 30 per cent at the open. The reversal followed a campaign in which President Trump pressed the board, and it lifted Wall Street and sent Asian markets sharply higher after a week in which the AI sell-off had pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction. The rebound did not end the scrutiny. The US blacklisted Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian firms over alleged Nvidia chip diversion, and the probe into Huang's former executive, Alice Huang, is widening, with senators demanding testimony from Commerce and Treasury officials.

The relief rally came alongside a sharp warning from the Federal Reserve. New York Fed president John Williams said inflation remains too high and hinted at a rate rise at the December meeting, a view Governor Christopher Waller may go beyond. Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase. Europe and the Gulf also dominated the news. Russian cruise missiles crashed in Poland, a Russian cargo ship burned in the Gulf of Finland, and Nato met urgently in Brussels. Iran-linked tensions also continued at sea, with tankers reported to have hit mines in Hormuz, though oil prices fell to near three-month lows.

At home, Andy Burnham's reset deals with the EU drew both praise and fierce opposition, and the Antalya COP31 climate talks collapsed over fossil fuel language. Democrats won their largest House majority since 1992.

editions.notification: Markets in correction after an AI-led rout, even as Anthropic's record IPO trades. Here is what is driving it.
editions.intro:
The AI share sell-off dominates the day. The S&P 500 closed at 6,918.45 on Friday, down 3.59% and in correction, its seventh straight losing session and longest such run since February 2020. The Nasdaq has erased its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the fall, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%. Anthropic's $81bn IPO, the largest ever, has been caught in the rout: it opened at $111.50, closed its debut at $97.17 and fell about 9% on Friday. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index recording its steepest weekly drop in decades. Regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have responded with emergency steps, including Taiwan's wider short-selling ban, but South Korea's KOSPI still fell 5% on Monday despite pledges of stabilisation funds.

Behind the sell-off are worries about debt-funded AI spending. Reports that Nvidia's $100bn OpenAI deal may not proceed, and reports that Anthropic has around $900bn of spending commitments that could be rated junk, have revived fears of a bubble. Nvidia's leadership is also in turmoil. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive US intelligence has reportedly linked to Chinese espionage. Bessent now says he would not oppose a return, though Colette Kress remains interim chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under growing pressure over chip sales to China.

Away from markets, Andy Burnham's UK-EU reset deals on trade, emissions and youth mobility are drawing fire, with student fees still unresolved. Democrats won their largest House majority since the early 1990s. A Lean verification of an Anthropic claim on the Riemann hypothesis adds a notable tech story, though it still needs human review.

Markets are the main story. Anthropic's $81bn Nasdaq debut at $83 a share was the largest IPO on record, but the shares have since slid and the wider AI trade has sold off hard. The Gulf and Ukraine are the other pressure points. On the diplomatic side, Trump, Xi and Putin met at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, but produced only a broad four-point declaration and no breakthroughs on nuclear arms. Europeans fret about being sidelined. Meanwhile a Russian cruise missile crashed in Poland during a NATO exercise, and Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge again.

At home, Andy Burnham signed a reset deal with the EU covering food, carbon trading and a youth mobility scheme for up to 100,000 people a year. Farage and Badenoch attacked it, and the EU has tied parts of it to tuition fees for EU students. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, and the Bank of England has raised rates to 4%.

editions.intro:
Attention in Shenzhen is on the first in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, due on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The White House has confirmed the trilateral, which is expected to focus on nuclear arms control after New START expired in February, though China has not formally confirmed it and Moscow says the format is not yet agreed. A senior US official said no agreement is expected. Trump has left the summit early, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent representing the US at some sessions. Beijing has called the meeting groundbreaking, while critics describe it as a "New Yalta" moment.

The wider conflict is adding pressure. Iran has fired drones and missiles at US sites in Bahrain and Kuwait after American strikes, and a Hormuz tanker fire has put a US-Iran memorandum at risk. Ukraine has partly collapsed the Crimean Bridge, and a third attack reportedly hit it on the same week. Separately, Nvidia has posted record revenue under interim chief Colette Kress, but its board has ruled out Jensen Huang's return, and Washington has widened AI chip export curbs, with Congress now moving to tighten them further.

Markets are dealing with several strands at once. Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 a share, making it the largest stock-market debut on record, with trading on the Nasdaq due on Thursday. Gold has fallen to its weakest level since September 2025 as markets price a possible US rate rise, and Deutsche Bank has fallen sharply after a leak of internal records. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign an EU food and farming reset at a Friday summit, which he says shows Brexit "has not worked".

Finance.title: Nvidia's Huang returns as CEO; AI stocks rebound in Asia
Finance.notification: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia and the AI trade is bouncing. Here is what it means for markets.
Finance.summary:
Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive less than two weeks after he resigned, following a campaign that included direct pressure from President Trump. Nvidia shares jumped roughly 30 per cent at the open, adding close to $1tn in value and lifting the Nasdaq and Dow. The rebound spread to Asia, where Taiwan, Korea and Japan rallied sharply after a week in which the Nasdaq suffered its worst weekly drop since 2020.

The reversal does not settle the questions. Investigations by the SEC and the Department of Justice continue, lawmakers want answers, and a separate US blacklisting of Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other firms over alleged chip diversion shows export controls remain a live risk. Reports also suggest the episode may open a route for Nvidia to sell AI chips into China.

Underneath the bounce sits a larger worry: whether debt-funded AI spending can pay off. Anthropic's record IPO was followed by a sharp tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 into correction, and reports of a shaky Nvidia-OpenAI deal and Anthropic's heavy spending commitments keep that concern alive.

World.title: Burnham's EU reset faces test as UK legislation nears
World.notification: Burnham's EU reset is signed, but fees, a Commons vote and rejoin talk now stand in the way.
World.summary:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's package of three deals with the EU, agreed in Brussels on Friday, is the biggest story in this section. It covers food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme allowing up to 100,000 18-to-31-year-olds from each side to live and work in the other. The EU says the deals will not take effect until tuition fees for EU students in British universities are settled, within six months, and London has reportedly offered £12,000 against up to £38,000 now. Legislation is due in Parliament next week.

The reset is also drawing fire from the start. Former prime ministers Theresa May, David Cameron and Tony Blair have warned against rejoining the EU, and Reform UK and the Conservatives have vowed to attack the deal. Burnham has not ruled out a future referendum but says there is "no fixed destination". Markets have reacted only modestly, with sterling mixed and UK consumer and utility shares firmer.

Beyond Westminster, the wider story is Russia's war spilling into Europe. A Russian cargo ship was set alight by drones in the Gulf of Finland, Russian Kh-101 missiles came down in Poland, and NATO's North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday. In the US, Democrats' largest House majority since 1992 sets up divided government, while the Federal Reserve signals a possible December rate rise.

Tech.summary:
Anthropic's record Nasdaq debut is the biggest story in tech today. The Claude maker closed its first day of trading about 17% above its IPO price, valuing it at roughly $1.7tn, after raising around $81bn in the largest IPO in history. The gains came against a weak backdrop: US indexes hit seven-month lows and Asian shares slid, as investors questioned whether AI spending will pay off.

That worry runs through a string of stories. Taiwan has widened its short-selling ban after the Taiex's worst week since 1991, emerging-market stocks are heading for a loss that would wipe out their 2026 gains, and a sharp US sell-off earlier in November hit chipmakers hardest. Commentators are also asking whether the AI build-out is crowding out the rest of the economy.

Nvidia is under pressure on several fronts. The Alice Huang chip-smuggling probe is widening, with scrutiny reaching Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Jensen Huang's return to the company remains under investigation. Meanwhile, a Lean-verified claim that Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis has drawn attention, though full human verification will take time.

Tech.notification: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, wiping up to $601bn off the chipmaker's value in a day
Tech.summary:
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker worth roughly $4 trillion. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of relationships with a woman US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security and with a direct report, and the shares fell as much as 14% in early trading.

The fallout is spreading across the sector. Democratic senators have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports say the Commerce Department stalled action against Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of routing chips to China. Investors are now focused on Nvidia's third-quarter results on 17 November, the first without Huang, and on whether the AI boom's financing web, which Huang helped build, holds up.

Beyond Nvidia, the sector is under pressure from a broad tech sell-off, AI-linked concerns in US midterm politics, and a heavy pipeline of listings. Anthropic's S-1 filing shows revenue growing very fast, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though with much larger losses.

Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years leading the chipmaker, following admissions of affairs, one with a woman US intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy and one with a company executive who reports to him. Nvidia shares fell sharply, and the wider AI trade has been unsettled by fears that a new leader could scale back the company's financing of customers and slow the AI build-out.

The episode also reaches into Washington and Taipei. A Republican senator has called for Huang to go, the House chairman says Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, and Taiwan is examining the woman's visits. Chinese AI firms are reportedly rushing to secure Nvidia capacity in case US rules on remote chip access tighten. Analysts will watch governance and export-control moves closely.

Beyond the chip story, the wider news is dominated by the Middle East and Ukraine. Oil rebounded after Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal, while Witkoff and Kushner met Putin, who signalled no compromise. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties is dividing Westminster ahead of a Brussels summit.

Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: Anthropic's record IPO reshapes AI market mood
Tech.notification: Anthropic closed its record Nasdaq debut about 17% higher, valuing it near $1.7tn, as AI stocks wobble.
Tech.summary:
Anthropic's record Nasdaq debut is the biggest story in tech today. The Claude maker closed its first day of trading about 17% above its IPO price, valuing it at roughly $1.7tn, after raising around $81bn in the largest IPO in history. The gains came against a weak backdrop: US indexes hit seven-month lows and Asian shares slid, as investors questioned whether AI spending will pay off.

That worry runs through a string of stories. Taiwan has widened its short-selling ban after the Taiex's worst week since 1991, emerging-market stocks are heading for a loss that would wipe out their 2026 gains, and a sharp US sell-off earlier in November hit chipmakers hardest. Commentators are also asking whether the AI build-out is crowding out the rest of the economy.

Nvidia is under pressure on several fronts. The Alice Huang chip-smuggling probe is widening, with scrutiny reaching Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Jensen Huang's return to the company remains under investigation. Meanwhile, a Lean-verified claim that Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis has drawn attention, though full human verification will take time.

Finance.title: Nvidia's Huang returns as CEO; AI stocks rebound in Asia
Finance.notification: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia and the AI trade is bouncing. Here is what it means for markets.
Finance.summary:
Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive less than two weeks after he resigned, following a campaign that included direct pressure from President Trump. Nvidia shares jumped roughly 30 per cent at the open, adding close to $1tn in value and lifting the Nasdaq and Dow. The rebound spread to Asia, where Taiwan, Korea and Japan rallied sharply after a week in which the Nasdaq suffered its worst weekly drop since 2020.

The reversal does not settle the questions. Investigations by the SEC and the Department of Justice continue, lawmakers want answers, and a separate US blacklisting of Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other firms over alleged chip diversion shows export controls remain a live risk. Reports also suggest the episode may open a route for Nvidia to sell AI chips into China.

Underneath the bounce sits a larger worry: whether debt-funded AI spending can pay off. Anthropic's record IPO was followed by a sharp tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 into correction, and reports of a shaky Nvidia-OpenAI deal and Anthropic's heavy spending commitments keep that concern alive.

World.title: Burnham's EU reset faces test as UK legislation nears
World.notification: Burnham's EU reset is signed, but fees, a Commons vote and rejoin talk now stand in the way.
World.summary:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's package of three deals with the EU, agreed in Brussels on Friday, is the biggest story in this section. It covers food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme allowing up to 100,000 18-to-31-year-olds from each side to live and work in the other. The EU says the deals will not take effect until tuition fees for EU students in British universities are settled, within six months, and London has reportedly offered £12,000 against up to £38,000 now. Legislation is due in Parliament next week.

The reset is also drawing fire from the start. Former prime ministers Theresa May, David Cameron and Tony Blair have warned against rejoining the EU, and Reform UK and the Conservatives have vowed to attack the deal. Burnham has not ruled out a future referendum but says there is "no fixed destination". Markets have reacted only modestly, with sterling mixed and UK consumer and utility shares firmer.

Beyond Westminster, the wider story is Russia's war spilling into Europe. A Russian cargo ship was set alight by drones in the Gulf of Finland, Russian Kh-101 missiles came down in Poland, and NATO's North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday. In the US, Democrats' largest House majority since 1992 sets up divided government, while the Federal Reserve signals a possible December rate rise.

Fashion.title: Dior's Hyunjin deal and Galeries Lafayette, with Bulgari remembered
Fashion.notification: Dior signs Stray Kids' Hyunjin as ambassador for beauty and Jonathan Anderson's collections.
Fashion.summary:
Dior has made one of the most notable moves of the day, signing Stray Kids member Hyunjin as a brand ambassador for its beauty division and for creative director Jonathan Anderson's collections. The deal, announced on Friday, lands as the group's world tour runs through July 2027 and reflects how luxury houses still lean on K-pop stars to reach younger buyers in Asia and beyond.

The wider industry is also marking the death of Paolo Bulgari, the third-generation figure who joined the family jeweller in 1960, became chairman in 1984 and helped turn the Roman house into a global luxury name before LVMH bought control in 2011. Coverage of his death has been consistent across outlets, and no new developments have emerged since the announcement.

Elsewhere, the business side is busy. Galeries Lafayette reported 3.1 billion euros of 2025 revenue, with chief executive Arthur Lemoine betting on stores as destinations even as French protests have hit Saturday trade. Louis Vuitton is opening an experiential flagship in Hong Kong on 12 December, and Ferragamo has taken direct control of its Puerto Rico retail after a 6.2 per cent fall in third-quarter sales.
